utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to be sure that the interpretation booths are working properly. First of all, let me turn to the Registrar. Do you hear what I am saying? Does the Prosecutor hear me? Do the assistants hear? The person who is working on the transcripts, do you hear? Yes. Do my colleagues hear me? All right. Mr. Marro, would you please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case IT-95-13-R61, the Prosecutor of the Tribunal against Mrksic, Sljivancanin and Radic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will now continue listening to the witnesses. I give the floor to the Prosecutor to bring in the first witness and to make the statements that we would like this person to make to the Tribunal. I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Clint Williamson on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. I am assisted today by Miss Ann Sutherland in court. At this time the Prosecutor would request a brief recess in this matter, an adjournment, until 2 o'clock this afternoon. My co-counsel, Mr. Niemann, has been taken ill this morning. We do not think that it is anything serious, but he has gone to a doctor and he should be back and able to proceed this afternoon, but we would ask the court's indulgence for a brief adjournment until that time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I will speak for a moment with my colleagues. Mr. Williamson, first, the Tribunal wishes a good and speedy recovery to Mr. Niemann. We will suspend the hearing but only until 2 o'clock. The hearings and the questioning of the 11 witnesses have already been announced. We had planned to listen to them during the course of 26th, 27th and 28th March. The Tribunal, therefore, does grant you this adjournment, but at 2 o'clock the Tribunal wishes to start again and that there be no further interruptions. For now we will adjourn the meeting until 2 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Legal assistants, everybody is ready to return. The Registrar, would you record the number of the case on the record, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is the case IT-95-13, Rule 61, Prosecutor of the Tribunal against Mrksic, Radic and Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Registrar. I would like to record that we are in the 61 hearing, and that this hearing will deal with the charges against the three accused whose names have just been recorded by the Registrar, the Prosecutor who has decided to call witnesses. The hearing was suspended this morning. We are pleased to note that Mr. Niemann has returned to us, and we give the floor to him immediately. The floor is yours, Mr. Niemann, and we would like to know whether we are now talking about witnesses which are those who were asking for protection. I give the floor to you, prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I am grateful for your Honours' indulgence this morning. Your Honours, the organisation of the witnesses will go back to what was originally planned, and so the protection measures will apply to those witnesses with the exception of Dr. Striber who has sought protection. Your Honours, I call the first witness, Dr. Vesna Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, do you mean that the protection measures that the Tribunal took will be extended to other witnesses as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: One other witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that we had decided as for witnesses A and B and then another witness who does not wish to have his identity protected, but does wish to have both his face and voice hidden. That was the order, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Has the Office of the Prosecutor decided that it will ask for other protective measures for any others. If that is the case, as the presiding judge, I am not going to refuse the request, but, first, I would have to confer with my colleagues and to be assured that the Prosecutor has made his position clear as regards the first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, with respect to the first witness, Bosanac, there is no application to be made at all. My colleague Mr. Williamson has had some discussions with other witnesses. I think once we have concluded with the witness Dr. Bosanac, then I will ask him to inform the Chamber of the current position with respect to any other witnesses in which protective measures are sought. So, if your Honour has no objection to that course, that is the way I wish to proceed. Dr. Bosanac, there is no application at all made in relation to her.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. I will just ask for a moment. Mr. Niemann, the Tribunal has decided to grant your request. If you would like to, I would ask the Registrar to help me where necessary. Each time a witness is called or cited, we would like before that witness even comes to the court, would you tell us what kind of protection he wants and we ask the Registrar to prepare the order which I can sign in accordance with my colleagues who will grant the kind of protection that has been asked for. Things are now clear. You can bring in the first witness who is not being protected in any way, nor is he having his voice or face hidden. So this witness can now come into the courtroom. The windows in front of the public gallery are open and he is invited to make his solemn declaration before begins to speak. So bring him in, please. Dr. VESNA BOSANAC called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: First of all, ma'am, do you hear me? Do you hear the Tribunal speaking to you? Do you hear us? Perhaps the Bailiff can make sure that the channel is turned to the proper place. Do you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You do hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does everybody hear me? Would you please rise, and tell us what your name is, what is your first name, what you do, and answer the Prosecutor's questions when he asks them. Please read the solemn declaration before you begin to speak. Who are you, ma'am, and would you please then make your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Vesna Bosanac. I am a medical doctor from Vukovar. I live currently in Zagreb and I work outside of the general hospital, and I am still head of the general hospital in Vukovar in exile.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Could you please read the declaration which was given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, nothing but the truth and the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. You can sit down now. This is the first witness. Could we please ask the Bailiff to remain close to the person who is speaking, at least in the beginning, in order to hand the declaration to that person and to make sure that it is in compliance with the Rules of our Tribunal so that everything goes smoothly as it ought to. The Tribunal is now asking to speak to us in serenity and as the Prosecutor will ask you to, please, answer the questions. This is an international criminal Tribunal in which you can speak with serenity and in full freedom. The floor is now yours, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Bosanac, were you born in Subotica in Vjovodina in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you a doctor of medicine?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you earn your Doctor of Medicine degree at the University of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After that did you work at the "Sveti Duh" Hospital and then were you subsequently transferred to the Vukovar Medical Centre?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That was in February 1974?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is your specialisation paediatrics?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you work from 1978 to 1979 at the Osijek General Hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you do two years, 1979 to 1981, at the Zagreb Hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you currently a paediatrician at the Children's Clinic at Kliepka(?) in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At the same time are you the director in exile of the Vukovar General Hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you also an advisor to the Minister of the Ministry of Health in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you appointed as the director of the Vukovar General Hospital on 25th July 1991?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At the time the war in Vukovar had started, were you the director of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: The war in Vukovar started earlier than that. It started on 2nd May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When the shelling started in the city of Vukovar itself, was that round about July 1991?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At that stage, I think, on 25th July, later on you became the director of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, it was on 25th July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us when the shelling started to hit the middle of the town of Vukovar, what month of the year was that, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: It was at the beginning of August, around 5th August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you recall the first occasion when the hospital was hit by the shelling?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: The hospital was hit, that is, the administrative building of the hospital, the hospital was hit by a shell around 7th August. It destroyed our record section but nobody was hurt at that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When this rocket hit the administrative building of the hospital, did you contact anyone about this event at the time?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I informed about this Government's Commissioner for the municipality of Vukovar, the Minister of Health and I also talked to the Commander of the barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army in Vukovar, Captain Ristic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In particular, speaking to Captain Ristic, did he tell you anything about the shelling or did he give you any assistance when you rang him?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No, he did not. I simply asked him the explanation for that but he did not answer anything specifically, because the administration of the building -- the hospital, the administration building was very close to the building where JNA officers live, and a shell fell on their garages as well. After that date, all officers were evacuated from the centre of the town and they withdrew to the southern part of the town to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is this the JNA barracks in the southern part of the town?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you recall the direction that the shelling was coming from at the time that the administration building of the hospital was hit, from what direction they were being fired?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: We thought that it came from the direction of Borovo Selo, but I cannot claim that with absolute certainty; whether it was from the direction of Borovo Selo or from the other bank of the Danube River.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On 24th August 1991 were some Serb soldiers injured around Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Actually, those soldiers were soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army who kept passing through the town in an APC and they went to -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We do not have the transcript on our monitors. Excuse me for a moment, please. We seem to have lost the transcript. The screen should now be working. All right, Mr. Niemann. We can resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What shall we do about the transcript? Is it all right now? It is back on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is back on our screen.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We return the floor back over to the Prosecutor now. MR. NIEMANN (To the witness): Dr. Bosanac, you were telling us before the interruption about the fact there were some JNA soldiers who were injured on 24th August 1991 in Borovo Selo. Would you tell us what happened to those soldiers when they were wounded?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: To the extent I am informed about that, those soldiers were driving in an APC. They were travelling from Borovo Selo in the direction of Vukovar and they turned from the road and hit a mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And ----

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Operation defenders then brought the four wounded soldiers to us, to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Once they were brought to the hospital, what happened then? What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: One of them was seriously wounded and he was burnt from the explosion and the other three were only slightly wounded, and they were given the necessary medical assistance right away. We gave them medicines, infusion and placed them under medical treatment. But shortly after that I was contacted by telephone by Captain Ristic from the JNA barracks and he requested that the soldiers be evacuated to the barracks. I told him that we could not do that because they had just been wounded and that they had to rest and receive medication, and they had to stay in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did Captain Ristic say to you when you said they could not be discharged from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: At that time he did not say anything any more, but he probably called our Chief of the Police and Government's Commissioner because he called me -- I was then called by the Chief of Police who told me that Captain Ristic insisted that we should prepare those wounded soldiers for the evacuation to the barracks. They wanted to transfer them to Belgrade from there, from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just for the record, who was at that time the Chief of Police in Vukovar? Can you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, I do, it was Mr. Stipa Pole.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After he contacted you and said that they must be released, what happened then? What was the next thing to happen?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Well, then we prepared them, well, actually I said that we could give them one ambulance and that they should send us a van or some other vehicle for the lightly wounded ones. So after that, after one hour maybe, an APC arrived at the hospital compound. It was closed down, and the janitor called me out and I got out and I saw that there was an APC in the hospital yard and I knocked at their lid and then an officer came out, but he did not get out of the vehicle, he just peered out, and then I asked him why he came to the hospital in a military APC, and then he said that he came to escort those wounded soldiers. He had a video camera and he recorded the hospital yard, and I told him that he did not have to come to the hospital in an APC, that we had been informed about everything and that the soldiers were ready for evacuation if they had to go, but that this was by no means good for them. Then the APC left the hospital premises, and a military van arrived with their driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At the time were there any military installations of any sort in the hospital ground or around the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did anyone accompany these wounded soldiers that were taken away in the ambulance, anyone from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, the ambulance was driven by our driver, and our nurse accompanied them, Anto Janko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When the nurse came back from where they were taken, did she tell you what had happened to the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, she did. She came back and she told me that there was a helicopter in the yard of the barracks and that Belgrade TV was there, and there were many people waiting for the wounded soldiers inside the barracks, and then they were transferred from our ambulance to the helicopter and they let her go back to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, were there any other JNA soldiers as patients in the hospital at that time apart from these men that were brought in who had been wounded in the APC?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No, that day, no, there were none, but before that soldiers used to come to our emergency section if they were ill and that was the first time that the wounded were brought there, wounded soldiers from the JNA. After that very often Croatian defenders brought captured wounded JNA soldiers to the hospital. So at the end of the war there were about nine who were treated in our hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, apart from the damage that had been done to the administration building of the hospital, up until this time -- this is up until 24th August 1991 -- had any other attacks, I call it that, been made upon the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes. There were attacks in the vicinity of the hospital, several shells hit the vicinity of the hospital, but it was only after that date that the hospital building was hit almost daily by shells and it was bombed from the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is it true that from 25th August 1991, that is, the next day after these soldiers had been removed, was the hospital itself bombed?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, were there any signs or markings on the hospital or in the vicinity of the hospital such as to indicate that it was a hospital if it was to be looked at from the air?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There was a sign on one of the buildings of the hospital, because the hospital had several buildings inside one yard, and one building had a red cross sign on the roof, and between the old and the new building, just on top above the nuclear shelter, we had placed a linen cloth sign, a very big one, very visible, bearing the Red Cross sign in white linen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Despite the existence of these signs was the hospital, notwithstanding that, attacked after 25th August 1991?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, it was attacked almost daily, and throughout October and November the hospital itself was hit between 150 and 200 shells a day. It was bombarded several times from planes, and two big bombs which weighed 250 kilos fell, hit the hospital directly and damaged it very badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you complain to anyone about the fact that the hospital was being attacked?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I lodged protests every day, I lodged appeals by telephone, by fax, over the radio, in my reports. I sent appeals to the Minister of Health, to the Croatian office in Hotel "I" in Zagreb where the European monitor mission was. I appealed to the international Red Cross in Geneva as well, and also using all kinds of media via Slovenian television, for example, through Croatian media as well, and I asked the Centre for Information in Zagreb to be connected by telephone to the general staff of the JNA in Belgrade. I made protests every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In particular, the protests to the JNA officers, did that achieve any cessation of the bombing of the hospital for you?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No, it was to no avail. It was as if I did not say anything. They just kept telling it was not possible, that the JNA would never do such things, and we could clearly see that the projectiles were being dropped from planes and the other bank of the Danube River from Petrova Gora (where the JNA was) and as of 1st October Vukovar was completely encircled, blockaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, what, if anything, did you do with the patients at the hospital in order to protect them from this constant artillery and bombing attacks?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Well, as early as August we organised -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are not actually receiving any translation. I am sorry about this technical problem but I cannot hear anything in my headphones any longer. I can not hear any Serbo-Croat and no French -- I have tried both channels. Now I can hear you. Thank you very much. That is fine. Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, in August 1991, when the first shells hit the town, we cleared up and prepared the shelter under the hospital building where we could move the patients. It was an underground shelter. So we worked and we spent all the time working in the basement in very improvised conditions, and we also practically lived and worked in the nuclear shelter. Before Vukovar was completely blockaded, at the time it was still possible to go through the cornfields, we were able to evacuate the wounded every day to Vinkovci and Osijek, but from 1st October it was not possible for us to send our wounded anywhere. It was very risky because the JNA soldiers or the Serbs who had weapons kept firing at ambulances as they were leaving the town and transporting the wounded. So the hospital was equipped so that we would have enough room for the wounded who were first surgically treated. So, after that initial treatment they were sent to some other shelters, to Borovo Selo, for example, in the factory where they had some very good nuclear shelters. We also placed them in residential buildings which had good nuclear shelters, so that is how we did it. We kept sending our wounded patients, or those who felt a bit better or those who were only lighted wounded, we sent them away from the hospital because it was impossible to keep all of them in the hospital. The hospital admitted daily an average of 60 wounded. One day we admitted only 12 patients and the greatest number was 92 patients one day. Most of them were civilians. Because they would leave their homes in the morning to get some food or water and Vukovar was constantly shelled, shells simply rained on the town every day especially at the centre where we were. The centre is about 10 kilometres away and every day there were about 7 to 9,000 shells that hit the town daily, and every day there were several attacks from the air as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, I think you said earlier in evidence that on one occasion, I think 4th October 1991, two bombs hit the hospital, one exploded and the other one travelled down through the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, both fell on the roof of the hospital, but one bomb, as soon as it dropped, it fell through the roof and exploded in the attic destroying totally, completely, three hospital rooms on the second floor. That was our surgical ward. The entire hospital building shook. There were some splinters of glass and dust. There was also smoke and stench from the hospital. We all rushed there to see if there was any fire burning, because we felt that there was an explosion. However, then somebody said that the bomb actually fell on to the shelter, so we went to the shelter. This is the entrance, the back entrance, to this shelter. You can see this very well on the video because I think you cannot describe it so clearly. So that second bomb went through the roof of the attic and then through three slabs of concrete and then fell on to a bed on which a patient was lying. Luckily, it fell on to that bed by his feet and the bed broke, collapsed, and it seemed as if the man was, sort of, riding on top of the bomb, unexploded bomb. The patient was totally shocked, he could not speak, while the medical nurse who was near him was also very shocked. All of this happened within seconds and she just thought that this was a cylinder, oxygen cylinder, that fell; in fact, it was a large bomb, aircraft bomb -- as large as this desk in front of me now. It was 250 kilos heavy and it did not explode. Then I called the Police Inspector to see, check whether the bomb was dangerous, whether it would explode later or not. He said: "No, it will not explode". So people put it on stretchers and took it out. First of all, we, of course, took the patients and then they took the bomb out into the backyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, apart from the air bombs that were dropped, can you describe, from the best of your recollection, the other types of bombs that you can recall that were being dropped in and about the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: There were quite a number of bombs of all kinds and descriptions. We saw only remnants of the unexploded bombs. Some of them fell but did not explode. We had a Police Inspector who was in charge of checking on these things. He would always come. He would check to see if there was any danger that some of the shells would explode subsequently. There were also some kind of bullets like clusters. Then from the aircraft some sort of small parachute, the parachute objects, made of metal and plastic material with some kind of powder in them and a sort of gas came, something hazy something like fog, and smelling of DDT. People were very much afraid that these might be poisonous gases, but it was found later that, in fact, these bombs and shells contained some kind of mild poison, but the effect was supposed to be mostly psychological. Also, some phosphorous bombs, fire bombs or fire grenades, fell that exploded and caused an immediate conflagration of fire. One such bomb or shelter fell on the roof which was dangerous. We had to go quickly upstairs and then, of course, put out the fire so that we do not get the panic in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was anyone injured as a result of these phosphorous bombs that you can recall from those times?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, I remember a girl who was brought to us who was all burnt, and we removed her clothes, shoes, and after half an hour the boots still had some kind of vapours coming out of the boots and had a very strong smell like sulphuric acid. She was very badly burnt. We took the physiological solution, infusions. We put on vaseline. We thought she would never survive. But we kept her clothes, remnants of her clothes, to establish later what kind of bomb that was, but all of this was left in the hospital when we were taken away. But I must say, luckily, the girl survived and she is all right now, but for two days after she left, the room in which she was lying had this very terrible stench. This was a very bad odour of this inflammable material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, you have said that you maintained your protests to various international agencies, such as the European Community monitoring mission that was located in Zagreb; that you rang various people in the Government in Croatia as well as you maintained contact with various peoples in the JNA itself. Did you also attempt to speak to people in Belgrade about what was happening to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, I tried to contact them by telephone. I called the office of the Yugoslav Prime Minister, Ante Markovic, who was at the time the Prime Minister. I did not actually get through to him. Then I asked for the Yugoslav army General of staff to contact them. Zivota Panic was the Chief of Staff. I wanted to talk to him, but then some assistants replied on the telephone and said that, I do not quite understand what I am saying, that it is quite impossible that their planes would ever hit the hospital and nothing changed at all. On one occasion I talked to General Raseta who was in Zagreb, who was representing the Yugoslav army in Zagreb, and I asked a wounded soldier who was a JNA solder -- his name was Sasa Jovic -- I asked him would he like to talk to the General to tell him the exact facts. He said: "Yes, I would". So he tried to convince the General that, indeed, the hospital was being hit, and I do not know what they said to each other, but I saw that the General asked him: "What do we have in the hospital? Do we have Croatian army?" He said: "No Croatian army, there are only wounded people here and medical staff", but despite all of this there was no change; the shelling never stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, were people in the community of Vukovar brought to the hospital when they were killed in the course of these attacks on the city?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: At first, when the war was not so bad, the ambulance would always go out, collect the wounded people, and bring them to the hospital. But, later all our ambulances were mostly destroyed and damaged, and the Croatian soldiers and the civilians would simply bring wounded people, dead bodies. They would all bring them to hospital because sometimes they did not even know whether the person was alive or dead; they thought we might be able to save lives, so sometimes they actually did bring dead people but our doctors could only declare them dead on arrival if they were dead. These people were then taken on the following day. First of all, the Police Inspector who was in charge of this, he took he made records of these people. He was like a coroner and he identified them as -- following the medical examination, he also conducted the police investigation. So, as I say, yes, both wounded and dead people were brought to the hospital compound; but not all of them, I must say, because sometimes they say: "We did not even know that he had been killed or how he died"; they simply buried him locally where they found him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, where were these people buried, the people that died at the hospital or were brought to the hospital dead, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Before the war became very bad or intense, we took dead bodies to the so-called Bulgarian cemetery, which was the official cemetery for the city of Vukovar, outside the city behind the Mitnica district in the direction of Vucedol. But in August when the shooting became very intense, the cemetery itself came under fire and it was not safe to go there to bury the people. Then we actually sent dead people to cemeteries, the old catholic and the old orthodox cemeteries which were both closer to -- which were close to the JNA barracks on the Sajmiste district of Vukovar. However, on one occasion in early October, the lorry that was taking dead bodies in coffins was actually hit from the JNA barracks, so that the drivers had to run for their lives leaving the lorry and the coffins there, and actually it was not possible to bury the people there either. Therefore, we dug a large grave not far from the old Jewish cemetery near Count Eltz chapel in the vicinity of the hospital and we continued to bury the dead people there. We buried them in coffins that were made in the Borovo factory. They were made from pieces of furniture -- wooden wardrobes were turned into coffins and so on -- and we buried them in three -- stacked three on top of each other, and we made records of them, we took numbers, so just as somebody was killed they were buried and somebody died and they were buried there. In the same grave we also had Croatian soldiers, civilians, and so on, but when that grave was filled, we tried to have to dig another grave between the football stadium and the railway line, but this was in open countryside, so to speak, so that the JNA tanks could shoot at the people directly across the Vuka River, so this became too dangerous as well. So, eventually we decided to transport, transfer the dead bodies to a building called Kapitanija just across the street from the hospital. This was a disused old people's home and this is where during the last two weeks of our stay there these people were buried in graves dug by hands, more or less, and they were simply wrapped in plastic foil. Again, we numbered them and buried people. I remember that during the last two weeks of our stay in Vukovar we had about 120 bodies that had to be buried, but we were told by the municipality that only a few people could be buried while large numbers remained unburied because there were people who were doing the burying had been attacked across the Danube River all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, on 10th November 1991, did some negotiations commence concerning the evacuation from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, that was the time when negotiations began between the European Commission, the International Red Cross, and the negotiated evacuation began which was supposed to be carried out by the organisation Medicines Sans Frontier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the purpose of these negotiations; what was sought to be achieved by them?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: The idea was that there would be a humanitarian corridor established through which the Vukovar Hospital could be supplied with basic supplies and medical aid for the blood transfusion and so on, because we needed those things very badly because we were very short of medical supplies because for two months practically we had no medical supplies arriving and our supplies had been allowed to run out. We did not have enough medicine, blood for transfusion and many other things that you need in a hospital to treat people, wounded people, and the people who were patients otherwise. Many civilians were in Vukovar. They were mostly women and children. We had 16 births and in the maternity ward we had three premature births in the nuclear shelter and we had no medicines to treat these young children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor when did ----

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: The corridor was expected then to bring us medicines and supplies. This should be done by the organisation of Medicines Sans Frontier, while at the same time the same organisation would be evacuating the wounded people, the patients and women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did the shelling of the hospital and its surroundings stop, cease, at what date, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: On 17th November, after that the hospital was not shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After the cessation of the shelling of the hospital, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: We expected the arrival of the International Red Cross and the European monitors. The European mission in Zagreb negotiated for their arrival and I was informed by telephone by our Minister of Health, and on 18th November at 8 o'clock the evacuation from the hospital was supposed to start. After that the civilians would also be evacuated. At that time, however, there was no shooting and shelling of the hospital any more, but we began to prepare for the evacuation, but large numbers of civilians from the shelters in the vicinity began to arrive into hospital. People heard over the radio that the corridor would be opened. They knew of the evacuation being prepared and so on. So they heard that the Croatian troops had left the town and they were very much afraid for their lives. They heard that the hospital would be evacuated and that the International Red Cross and the European Mission would arrive to evacuate people so that the hospital would be considered as neutral, so they came to us for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was your family with you at this time, on 7th/8th November?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No, no, on these days, no. My husband was in Borovo Naselje. He was in charge of the organisation for logistical support for electricity, for -- he was an engineer so he was in Borovo Naselje. My mother and my father-in-law and my mother-in-law were in the cellar of our house not far from the hospital, and I tried to visit them every day. Late in the evening when I finished I would go home and then would come back to the hospital in the morning, but I expected that when the evacuation started we would also manage to bring the whole family together so that we will be evacuated together under the protection of the International Red Cross, and we also thought that we would be able to evacuate people from the shelter. This was our reserve hospital with nine doctors and there were 14 nurses and about 150 people, injured people, wounded people, who we had sent from our hospital to that shelter which was a well organised shelter with electricity, food and water.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, when was the evacuation to take place? Had a date been agreed when this would occur?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: The agreed date was 18th November, 8 o'clock a.m. EC monitors and representatives of the ICRC were supposed to come to the hospital at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do in advance of 18th November, you and your staff do, in order to prepare for the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: On Sunday, on 17th November, we prepared the wounded for the evacuation. All those who had pins or some kind of extensions, we put plasters on their wounds so that they would be able to travel. We prepared, we drew up lists and medical documentation for all patients, for all the wounded. So, each wounded had a white plastic bag with him with his case history and the X-ray findings as well. Other case histories and medical documentation of those who were no longer in hospital, we prepared, we put that in one box and we were supposed to, as well as all our records, because we kept records of everything we did in hospital, operation reports and so on. So, all of our reports, we prepared everything and put it into a box and we expected that we would be able to take it with us for the evacuation. That is what we did on Sunday. I informed all doctors who were in charge of specific wards of the situation, so we made lists of patients and we wanted them to know, to declare, where they wanted to continue their medical treatment, because we had lots of wounded, lots of civilians as well, and several JNA soldiers in the hospital who wanted to continue their medical treatment in Novi Sad or Belgrade. So we made note of that so that we would be able to know how many vehicles we needed and what destination they will be going to. That is what we were doing on Sunday, on 17th November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the day of the planned evacuation on 18th November 1991, what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Nothing happened in the morning. Nobody showed up in the hospital. It was very quiet. There was no shooting going on, and we only heard some distant fire shells, but the very centre of the town was not hit; there was no shooting going on. So I phoned Zagreb and I wanted to know when they will arrive, why they were not coming. Minister Hebrang told me that he did not know anything for the time being, that he only knew that they had left but he did not know when they would arrive. A Red Cross team was supposed to come from the direction of Ilok and the other one across the Danube River by boat, and European monitors were supposed to come as well, but nobody showed up. At 11 a.m. the European monitors called me on the telephone and they told me that they were on their way to the hospital, they were in the village of Negoslavci, but that they could not go, they could not leave yet, because the Yugoslav People's army was telling them that the situation was not safe yet, that there was still shooting going on, but that they would arrive as soon as possible. So I told them there was no shooting here, that the situation was quiet and that they should come as soon as possible because people already started dying because of the gangrene. We had run out of medication and water and food.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So what did you then do when they had not arrived at the agreed time? What did you then do?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Nothing. I just wrote protests again. I sent faxes. I sent a fax on 18th to the European Mission and I requested for their arrival, but they did not come, and Minister Hebrang told me that he had heard that the International Red Cross were busy with the surrender of the Croatian civilians and soldiers at the southern part of the town, but that they would arrive at the hospital in the morning of the 19th. So we then waited for the 19th. So I called again because they did not arrive the next morning. I called General Raseta in Zagreb who was the representative of the Yugoslav People's army to see what was going on, what happened to them, because the monitors called me on the phone, had called me on the phone, the day before from Negoslavci so I knew that they there were around, so if there were people surrounding at the southern part of the town. So General Raseta told me that I should contact Colonel Mrksic and that he was in charge of Vukovar. I asked him how because I did not know where he was. So he said that Colonel Mrksic would find me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened after that, after he said that to you?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: So then I called again and Mrksic did call me once, and he said that they would be there shortly and I should not worry about it; Vukovar was now liberated and that there was no more war going on. So I protested and I told him that the situation was very difficult, and that we should start the evacuation immediately, that the wounded were dying and were in very bad condition. So I called Raseta again and he told me that he had information that the International Red Cross and the army had reached the bridge. That was on Tuesday, in the morning of Tuesday, on the 19th of November. So then Marin Vidic who was the Government's Commissioner for the municipality of Vukovar and my assistant, Stanko Voloder, as an interpreter, and myself, we went to the bridge on foot to find them. So we got there to the bridge, and it is a sort of an overpass above the railways in the direction of Borovo, and we saw many military lorries there, APCs, many soldiers, and Serbian paramilitary soldiers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This bridge, can you just describe it a little bit more for us, please, what was it a bridge over?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: It was the bridge in the direction of Borovo Naselje. It is a sort of an overpass over the railway lines, and it was not far from the hospital, maybe 300 metres away. That is where we saw all those soldiers, Serbs, Chetniks, that is where we saw them entering the town and loading civilians on to the lorries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you saw these JNA soldiers and other paramilitary people, did they say anything to you or did they notice you at all?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, they noticed us immediately because we had arrived from that part of the street and there was no-one there and I said that we were from hospital and I asked for their commander, so they shouted at one person and then an officer came. I asked him where the ICRC people were, and that we were told by General Raseta that they were supposed to come any moment. I was very afraid because the ICRC and monitors were not there, but the officer told me that he knew nothing about it, and that he was from the Novi Sad corps and that his assignment was to reach the bridge, and that they were not in charge of the area after the bridge at the hospital and this part of the town of Vukovar. So we went back to the hospital and we waited again. Then two hours later, around 12 o'clock clock maybe, a military industry vehicle came in front of the hospital, and then I got out again and I asked them where the ICRC people were. The person was a JNA officer and he told me that he knew nothing about it, that he had seen some white vehicles from an international organisation in the village of Negoslavci but that he knew nothing about the evacuation of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ask him then to do anything?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, I asked him if he could take me to Negoslavci so that I can find ICRC people and he said that he could. I then asked him if he could guarantee that no-one would enter the hospital until the arrival of ICRC people. So he asked him (sic) how many entrances there were to the hospital, and I told him there was one in the yard and I told him where the buildings were, and he said that he could guarantee the safety. He called some of his soldiers and told them to deploy around the hospital and that no-one should either enter or leave the hospital until we return.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then? What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: So I went back just shortly to the hospital and told my colleagues that I was going to Negoslavci to find the International Red Cross, and some of them tried to talk me out of it because they were very afraid, but I told them I had to go because we did not know when the international Red Cross people would arrive. So that is how I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then when you left?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: So we passed that area of the town which was completely destroyed. Just a second, please. We arrived in Negoslavci and I saw many soldiers there and many equipment, APCs, tanks, other vehicles, and they took me to a house. The house was just a family house, a residential building, but it had written "Headquarters" on it. So that is where they took me. There was another young man who was with me who spoke English, his name was Voloder, who was supposed to interpret for me if I find ICRC members. So we arrived there. They took me upstairs inside that house. They took me to a room where an officer was sitting and he said -- his name was Mrksic, Colonel Mrksic -- I told him I was Dr. Bosanac from the hospital and the General Raseta told me I should contact him, the International Red Cross members were not there and that the situation in the hospital was critical because many wounded were dying of the gangrene, and there were also some of their soldiers, JNA soldiers, in the hospital. He was surprised and he said: "What soldiers?" I told him that Jovic Sasa was there, among others. He was very surprised because he thought that those soldiers had been killed. I could see that he was glad that they were alive. He also told me that it was impossible to organise the evacuation which was signed by General Raseta because the situation in the field was completely different, but that we could organise an evacuation via Serbia, Sid, and the town of Sid, but I told him it was impossible because everybody was expecting us in Nustar because that was what the International Red Cross guaranteed, and they were all waiting for us in Nustar, and we were supposed to go to Luzac, Marinci, Bogdanovci and then to Nustar. Then he said ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry, did he say why you had to go via Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No, he did not tell me why; he just told me that the area before Nustar was mined and that their positions were there and that they had to clear the minefields, the JNA soldiers had to clear the mines so that we could pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you say to him then after that?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I told him that I did not understand much about that, but I knew that that was the agreement because the Minister told me on the telephone that an agreement had been signed and that we should go through Marinci, Bogdanovci, Nustar and Vinkovci because this territory was free territory of Croatia, and I simply could not believe how they would be able to take us to Serbia and it was impossible considering the fact that the town had been destroyed and shelled, and I could not simply imagine that they were going to take us to Serbia. I thought that the evacuation that was agreed in European mission should be -- that that agreement should be respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you also tell him that you needed the representatives of the International Red Cross and the European Community monitoring mission people there as well?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is why, and I told him that that was the reason why I had come to Negoslavci because I heard that they were there, and he told me that they were indeed around, but that they kept moving around and taking, drawing up some lists but that they were actually of no use and that we could do much more if we find an agreement. I told him that they should be in charge of that because they signed the agreement. So he said that as soon as he finds them that he would send them to the hospital, and that he would also send food and water to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: So then I ask him if I could return to the hospital and he said, yes, and as I was leaving the house, I saw in the street a white vehicle standing, belonging maybe to European monitor, so I asked the driver to take me to that vehicle but he said he could not, that he had to ask the Colonel again. So he went and then came back, and when he came back to me and Voloder, the interpreter, he said: "No, the Colonel said that I should not take you anywhere else now, that I should take you to the hospital and that you should wait there and that the International Red Cross people would arrive". Then he took us back to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you arrived back at the hospital, what did you find there at the time?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: On the way back to the hospital, I saw many civilians walking through the city, including my mother among them. I saw her, so I asked the driver to stop the vehicle and take me to our vehicle, and she said they were all being driven, that they should leave their shelters and their cellars because they would be throwing bombs or grenades in to there and they were all being sent to Velepromet compound. Also she said that my father and mother-in-law had already left because the father-in-law could not walk, he was being taken in a vehicle. Then we came back to the hospital and saw soldiers there surrounding the hospital, but I also saw one of our staff, one of our workers, who used to work in the hospital and who had joined the Serbian Chetnik group troops, and I saw him running around the hospital. Everybody was very much afraid of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. I would like to ask the witness if she is not too tired. The witness has been speaking for one hour and 10 minutes. I would like to know whether she would prefer that we have a break; if not, we can continue. I would also ask the Prosecutor to ask where we are in this testimony. There is also the issue of nervousness, so perhaps we could answer this question. I would like to ask you, Mrs. Bosanac, how do you feel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not tired, but I am shaken. I never thought I would find it so difficult to testify.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I would, therefore, propose, as confirmed by the emotions which we do understand, that we take a 15 minute break and resume in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Registrar, could you please ask the usher to show in the witness? Thank you. Mr. Prosecutor, the Tribunal has decided that to try to catch up with some of the lost time we will hear the witness or witnesses until quarter to five, so for another hour, and then we will take a break of another 15 minutes and, with your agreement and I would like to thank the interpreters who are here for also their agreement, we would then carry on this evening until quarter past 6 with your agreement. Prosecutor, quite clear, if you would prefer to pose your questions sitting, then the Tribunal would very well authorise you to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour, I am fine. (To the witness): Dr. Bosanac, just before the break you were telling us how you had returned to the hospital after seeing Colonel Mrksic, and when you arrived back there that there were JNA soldiers and paramilitary type people surrounding the hospital. I think you said that there was a state of great tension in the hospital at that time with the patients and the staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened when you returned? Can you carry on from there?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I got back to the hospital to my office, and I tried to calm down the people who were around me. I told them that we were expecting the International Red Cross so that we could agree on the evacuation of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were the JNA soldiers doing with the patients, with the people, at the hospital when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Some of the JNA soldiers remained at the hospital entrance to provide some sort of security, but some of them entered the hospital. Our former janitor who used to work in the hospital entered with them to see who was in the hospital. He greeted some people in the hospital, people who used to work with him before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you say anything to these JNA officers or these other people, these other people in uniform, that were there?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, I did. When, for example, a soldier wanted to enter the hospital with weapons, and my office was very close to the entrance, I would then approach him, get out, approach him and I would tell him that it was prohibited to enter the hospital with weapons. Once there was a group of soldiers, weirdly dressed soldiers with helmets and some White Eagles painted on their helmets. They were very aggressive towards me and they said that -- they asked who I was and that I had no business telling them anything. So then a doctor, a Serb, who used to work with us, Dr. Ivankovic, he got out of the hospital and he told them that they should not behave aggressively; he told them to calm down and he told me not to provoke them, to keep quiet, because otherwise it would be bad for us, and that I was director of the hospital, that I had been director of the hospital for too long a time, something like that. He told me, "You have been issuing orders long enough Vesna; you had better keep quiet now". That is what he said, but those soldiers with helmets then left. Actually, his son was with them. He went to visit his father and they left together. There were many people in the hospital because the previous two days lots of civilians arrived in the hospital. Zeljka Zgonjanin, who was the representative of the Croatian Red Cross organisation arrived, arrived at my office, and Marin Vidic was also with me in my office. She said that people were panicking, people who were on the first floor, they were mainly civilians. There was no longer any shooting so it was not dangerous to be on the first floor. So she came to me and she said that they were panicking because the soldiers started separating men from women and they started to take the civilians away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you speak to any of the senior JNA officers at that time or shortly after?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Well, then after -- when she told me that, I got out to see what was going on and I saw that on the other entrance of the hospital, the entrance which we did not use then, the entrance which was just closed in for the protection, and I saw they were taking away civilians through that entrance, so I asked them what was going on. That is when I saw Major Sljivancanin for the first time. I saw him there. So I approached him and I asked him where they were taking the civilians, and he said that they were being taken away for the purpose of getting listed down to the Velepromet shelter. He said that after that they would meet again with their families. I did not know him before, but he appeared -- he was, he appeared very arrogant to me and he did not pay too much attention to what I was saying, and I ask him when the International Red Cross would arrive, and that I was told that they would come as soon as possible, but that we have been waiting for them for two days. He said, well, they will show up eventually. It all happened around 5 o'clock p.m. It was still daylight. Then it was getting dark, and then this representative of the International Red Cross, Mr. Nicolas Borsinger arrived and one more doctor who said he was just a medical doctor working for the International Red Cross, and they were brought by Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Brought to where, where were these people brought?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: To the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened when they were brought to you? What did you say to them?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Well, I was in my office and they arrived to my office and Sljivancanin said, "Here they are, you have been asking for them for so long, now I have brought them to you". Then Mr. Nicolas came and he said that they had brought a truck full of medicine for us. At that time I was already very disappointed and I told him that we expected them, that we were waiting for them the day before for the purpose of the evacuation, and that the wounded are in a very bad condition, so I did not know what to do with the medicine that they had brought and that we were supposed to leave for the evacuation. Then he said that I should try anyway, that they could not arrive earlier, and he told me to use those medicines, if possible. So I sent our head nurse and a pharmacist to the lorry so that they can see if there is anything that we can use for the transport. So we passed through one part of the hospital to show them how difficult the situation was, and there were lots of wounded who had been waiting for very long for the evacuation. They were very tired and sick because they did not have adequate medicine, adequate treatment, or water or food for very long time. He said that he would come back the next morning and that we should start organising the evacuation. So I told him that I expected that he would stay, remain in the hospital, and that we were all very scared. So they asked us if we had lists of patients and we said we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say, "they asked you", who was "they" asked you for the list of patients?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: They were together in a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, but -----

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin, this Mr. Nicolas Borsinger, and another doctor whose name I do not know, but who worked for the International Red Cross and there was also a lady interpreter with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But do you remember which one of them, was it Major Sljivancanin that asked you for the list or was it the gentleman from -----

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it Mr. Nicolas that you were saying you wanted to actually stay at the hospital and not go away and come the next day?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I did not quite understand your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry. I think you said in your evidence that one of them said, and I am asking you whether it was Mr. Nicolas, that he would go away and then come back the next day, the 19th, in order to evacuate the patients?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because I expected that he would stay in the hospital now that they had arrived, but, no, he said, no. He said that they would leave and come back the next morning. He also asked him, and I was very surprised by that question, if I thought that it was absolutely necessary that they should come, and I said, "Of course, I expected them to stay here".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you give any copies of lists to either Mr. Nicolas or Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had on my desk four copies of the list of wounded who were treated in the hospital and who were ready for the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Major Sljivancanin say anything to you about the people on the list? Did he say anything about their condition?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Actually, I wanted to give to Mr. Nikolas one of the lists, one copy, and leave other three for us, because I wanted to take them for the evacuation together with the wounded, but Major Sljivancanin wanted me to give me -- to give him all of the lists, and I asked him, why, because the copies were all the same. He said that he wanted to check them. He also asked me if there were -- if the lists carried also medical staff, names of the medical staff, and I told him, no, and that I thought that it was not necessary to make a list of the medical staff and that we only needed the list of the wounded who were treated in the hospital. So he said that I should make also a list of the hospital staff. So I told the nurse and one of the administrative employee to make a list of medical staff, and also a list of lightly wounded who had come to the hospital together with the civilians and were on the first floor. They drew up a list in the evening, on Tuesday, but I think they never gave those lists to anyone. I do not know anything about that because I was no longer there after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened after that, after you had given these lists to Major Sljivancanin and Mr. Nikolas? What was the next event that occurred?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: When they left, they left the hospital, it happened in the evening of the 19th of November, Tuesday. So we just sat there, waited and the night fell, but then a young officer or a JNA soldier arrived and he told me that he had an order to take me to Negoslavci. I told him, "OK". I took my coat and my bag and I just thought that Mrksic wanted to see me again in a meeting to organise the evacuation. So I went to the vehicle with that soldier and he drove me to Negoslavci that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you arrived at Negoslavci what happened there at that place?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Well, I arrived in the same house, in the same house I had been during the day, and there was "Headquarters" written on it, and I was again taken to the same room upstairs. The only thing that was different was Mrksic was no longer there, but Major Sljivancanin and another officer, a captain -- I do not know his name -- and they told me to sit down. I asked them where Colonel Mrksic was and then Sljivancanin asked me why I asked him that. I told him that I expected Colonel Mrksic there because I had talked to him earlier. Then he told me that he already had another assignment and he again told me to sit down and talk. Then he asked me, well, then we talked for a while, and he asked me if I knew where Jastreb was. "Jastreb" was the nickname for the Commander of the Defence of the town, and I told him I did not know and that I had not seen him since last week. He asked me where other Croatian soldiers were, and I also told him that I no longer saw the ones I knew because they had already left. He was very angry and he asked me, well, if there are no Croatian soldiers here, who then killed his young soldiers -- young soldiers who had only joined the army, and I told him I did not know. I told him I was only a doctor and I had no military information whatsoever, and that I always tried to help people and that I did not understand why they came and why they had destroyed the city. This captain who was sitting there as well, he was very arrogant as well. He threatened me and he said that they knew me and that they had listened to all my conversations with Zagreb, and that they knew that I had called President Tudjman, the government and so on. I told him that that was correct and I told him that I had indeed called everyone and asked for help, any kind of help, and that I wanted the hospital -- I did not want hospital to be bombarded and I asked for supplies to be sent because we had run out of everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he say when you replied this way to Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Well, he said that he has all conversations recorded and that they have other methods, and that they could easily find out about my guilt. Then Major Sljivancanin asked me if I knew how much money President Tudjman was prepared to offer for me. I told him that I was convinced that he would not give anything because I was just an ordinary doctor, like all other doctors, and that there was actually no reason for him to pay for me. So then he asked me: "As a doctor, would you work in our war hospital with Serbs?" I said: "I do not know, probably yes", but I was very scared at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When he said how much would Tudjman pay, did you understand that to be how much ransom he would be prepared to pay for you?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you had this conversation, what else, what did they then say to you that would happen?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: He said: "OK, we would see about that tomorrow, and tonight you have to stay here". I asked him, I begged him, to take me back to the hospital and he said it was impossible, it was still very dangerous and there was still shooting going on. I said: "But it was not dangerous and that if I had been able to survive so far, I could as well go back to the hospital". Then he said that he would take me to their hospital which was housed in a elementary school building to spend the night there. A soldier took me there, to the school building in Negoslavci, to a room upstairs where there were four beds. So that is where I spent the night sitting on the bed. At 6 o'clock the next morning the same soldier came to pick me up, and he took me out and into a jeep, and Marin Vidic was already sitting in that jeep, so I realised that he had probably been interrogated. So they took us back to the hospital together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "the hospital", you mean your hospital, the Vukovar General Hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This date, the next morning, was the 20th of November 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: That is correct, Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You went back to the hospital; when you arrived back there what happened at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I came back to the hospital in the morning, it was before 7.00 in the morning. I went back to my office and a young officer came to my office. He had a weapon, a rifle of some sort, and he sat next to me all the time. He said that I should stay, that I had to stay there until further notice and that I could not make any telephone calls nor contact anyone. The telephone kept ringing, but he would not allow me to pick up the receiver and he answered the phone every time it rang. So we stayed like that for a while and some of my colleagues entered my office; they wanted to know what was going on. Everybody was afraid. I told them that we were expecting the Red Cross, and I was actually expecting Mr. Nicolas and I thought that we would be evacuated. But at that moment Sljivancanin arrived and he told me that I should ask all doctors to come to a meeting in a big room. So I called the head nurse and I told her to tell all chiefs of wards to meet in a plaster room which was a very large room and which was actually a makeshift operating theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was this room located, the plaster room?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: The plaster room was not far from my office, just next to the surgical ward, close to the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On what floor of the hospital was it?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: It was in the basement. As you enter the hospital through the emergency ward entrance, you turn to the left and that is where we had a surgical ward and the plaster room. Two thirds of that room are actually underground, but there is also a little window which are above the level of the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At approximately what time of the day was this?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: It was at 7.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then subsequently attend this meeting in the plaster room with your staff?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, we were there in the plaster room and Major Sljivancanin came and spoke to us. He said that the Yugoslav army had freed Vukovar, that it had taken the control of the hospital, that I am no longer the director of the hospital and that the evacuation will be in the hands of the military medical academy. He pointed to a few people in the room, there were doctors, the Yugoslav army doctors, but in uniforms, the Yugoslav army uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did -----

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I did not know these people, I must say. But he said that if somebody would like to stay and work for the hospital, continue working for the hospital, they could, but that I need not stay, I can go back to my room, he said. So I came back to my room indeed and hoped that I could wait there until the International Red Cross arrived. However, a young junior officer came who had been driving me to Negoslavci the previous evening and he told me that he was ordered to take Marin Vidic, the Government Commissioner for the municipality of Vukovar and myself, that he should take us to the place where the negotiations with the International Red Cross would take place. So we, indeed, left the hospital. I saw a number of our staff waiting there ready for evacuation. They were in their white medical uniforms, and we passed through them or between them as a corridor. Then a nurse asked me: "Madam, where are they taking you?" I said: "Well, to negotiations with the International Red Cross to arrange for the evacuation and I will be back soon", I said. I was, indeed, convinced that we would be taken to a meeting with the International Red Cross but they actually took us to the army barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say the "army barracks", do you mean the JNA army barracks that you referred to earlier in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you saw these people around the hospital, the staff that you have just referred to, were they just standing around in groups or in lines or were they being organised in any way? Did you notice anything like that?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No, as a group, sort of grouped around the entrance. This was no orderly arrangement. They were simply standing there, wasting their time, waiting for the evacuation. There was no order in that, but there were quite a number of people there. I saw many nurses. I saw also our drivers, men, all dressed in white overcoats. Then we had laboratory technicians, doctors. They were all huddled around the entrance. I would not say whether everybody was there or not. I cannot -- I could not notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the patients of the hospital? Were they there at the time or were they back inside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No, the patients were still in hospital, as far as I know. I saw no patients in the yard, in the grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about some of the people who had come up from the town to assemble at the hospital in the hope of being evacuated, were they there at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The French translation is breaking through and the witness hears French.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecutor, apparently, we have another technical problem with the interpreting channels.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now it is all right. The translation is all right now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, did you hear my question or would you like me to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What I asked you, doctor, was what about the people from the town that had assembled around the hospital in the hope of being evacuated, did you see any of those people at the time when you were taken away?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No. I think that most of these people had already been taken the previous day, on Tuesday, because as I was leaving the hospital I saw a small group of civilians not far from the emergency unit, but I did not see many people in the yard because I was walking in the direction of the main entrance and I did not see many people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Tell us then what happened when you went to the JNA barracks in the southern part of the town?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: When we arrived there, we entered the barracks. I had never been to that barracks before. We climbed the steps to the first floor. We were taken to a room where there was a soldier, a young soldier, with a white pistol or with a white holster for the pistol, probably military police. The junior officer who brought us there said that we should stay there, and that they would come and fetch us in about half an hour's time. He also told the young soldier, the military policeman, he said: "You stay here, do not leave the room and make sure that nobody either leaves this room or enters this room". That is what he said and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they, in fact, return in half an hour like they had promised?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No. The same man returned only at 6 o'clock in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So did you wait there all of the day, approximately all of the day?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When he returned at 6 o'clock in the evening what happened then?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I asked him: "Where have you been? You said you would be coming back in half an hour". He said: "Well, the plans have changed. The evacuation has already been completed". I said: "But where is the International Red Cross?" They said: "Yes, yes, they were there; everything was in order, but the plan was changed", and that we should stay there and spend the night there, not in the same room. So he took us to a large room with a number of empty beds, and he again told the same soldier to stay with us in the same room and make sure that nobody should enter or leave. Anyway, so we sat, each on one bed, and we were quite sure that we had been arrested. We just sat there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then after that?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Later in the evening, around 10 o'clock, he came back, the same soldier, and said I should go out. Marin also stood up. He said: "No, no, you stay there, you stay there, only the doctor should leave". So I followed the man. He took me to the ground floor, to a room where there were several officers and a woman in combat uniform. They said, they addressed me and said that I should make a statement for the Yugoslav army.
