I said: "A statement on what?" and they said about the situation in Vukovar, what had been done in Vukovar so that they could decide how to treat me and what to do with me. They asked me whether I would like to make that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Well, I said that I can make a statement. They asked, could they take a video recording and I said, yes, with a camera. So I said to them that I had been the director of the hospital, that everything was done in the interests of the patients and I gave the same kind of statement that I am making now to you, only it did not take that long. I spoke for 10 to 15 minutes describing the situation at the hospital as impossible, that it was most important to help people and patients and so on. The woman in that group told me that, according to their information, I was not doing only that and that they would have to check on that. So they took me out, out of the barracks. There was a police vehicle outside, a black vehicle. They opened the back door for me to go into the vehicle, and I saw a colleague of mine seated there already, that was Dr. Juraj Njavro, in his white overcoat and doctor's uniform and trousers, and sitting next to him was a technician who came as a volunteer from Zagreb. He came to Vukovar. That was Anto Aric. The door was closed and we were arrested again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you taken then?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: They took us within that car, we could not see where because they was only a small window in the front, but we saw that we were being taken out of Vukovar towards Sid and towards the motor way for Belgrade. So we drove on the motor way for Belgrade all the way to Belgrade, and we came to Trpinja, that is a district of Belgrade, and I know from earlier, I knew that that was the place where the barracks, the Yugoslav army barracks, in Belgrade were. We thought we were being taken for investigation and examination. We stopped there. I knocked on the door because I wanted to say I was going, I needed to go to the toilet, but nobody would open the door for me. They sat into the car again. We started again, turned back and returned the same way, the same way from Belgrade towards Mitrovica, the same motor way, but in the direction of Mitrovica. We came to Mitrovica in front of the Police building. They asked something. It seems that the drivers had no idea where they should be taking us, so they asked something at the Police Station, then brought us to a building that was a prison in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mitrovica is in Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the rest of your family? What had happened to them? Did you know?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No, I had no idea. I only knew that both of my sons were in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened? How long were you held in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 18 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did anything happen to when you were in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: This was, first of all, a great shock for me. We came to Mitrovica, that was a Thursday morning around 3 o'clock. As soon as we entered through the gate, some policemen dressed in black, two of them actually, started to beat us; first of all, the technician, Anto Aric, and they started beating him with fists. When he fell they also trampled on him, kicked him with feet. I could not watch that. I protested, but they were very arrogant and said I should turn towards the wall and keep quiet, but then they did stop beating him. They beat him for about three minutes, and so they left us standing there. Then a woman came wearing a Police uniform and she said I should follow her. So she took me to her room and said I must empty my bag and I must totally undress, that this is the procedure with prisoners and I found that very degrading. I asked whether I had been charged with any crimes. She did not say anything. I asked again: "Am I charged with something?" She said: "Ask the army". I said: "But then do call somebody, a soldier, officer on duty so I could ask him", but I had to stand there and I was very confused. She did leave and after about quarter of an hour an army officer came, and later I learned that he was the Lieutenant Colonel, but I learned later that he was the Stajicevo prison camp commander. I saw that he was rather sleepy when he arrived, that he had no idea what was happening. He was in a very kind of, with a -- he had a red beret on the head and the uniform was not full, not complete. He was about a 55 year old man, not a young man. Anyway, he came. I asked: "Am I now arrested? He said : "Who are you?" I said: "I am Dr. Bosanac from the Vukovar Hospital". He told me to sit down, to calm down. He gave -- he asked me to have a cigarette, while Dr. Njavro and Anto were standing in the corridor with a head leaning against the wall. So I sat down and I said I had no idea why I was there because we were medical people and what kind of procedure is that. I told him that Anto had been beaten and Dr. Njavro was an elderly man and suffered from ulcer, and his ulcer was bleeding, but he worked all day, the day before. He was a surgeon. I explained to the officer that we were medical people. He said: "Well, I do not know why you were brought here, but we will see in the morning and things would be clarified", he said. So he again called the prison guards to take us somewhere. The woman took me through the prison yard into some kind of cellar, or through some kind of cellar, into a basement cell, cell, solitary confinement cell, with a very heavy door and windows, barred windows, so that I was locked there for that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said a little earlier you stayed there for a further period of 18 days?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in the morning a woman came and brought a piece of bread and one boiled egg, and I asked her again to call the officer on duty. She did not say anything; she simply left. So, again after about an hour or two -- so that night for me was very awful. I heard many screams during the night and wailing. I did not know who was in prison. I never saw anybody but the three of us who were brought together. So, anyway, two officers came; one was Captain Zoric and the other was the one that was examining me when he was with Sljivancanin in Negoslavci that evening earlier. So these two came and said: "We understand that you wanted to talk to us". I said: "I wanted to talk to an officer on duty to simply ask what I have been charged with". They said: "Ah, you would like to talk?" I said: "Yes, of course I would like to talk because I do not know what to talk about, but I would like to know why I am here". He said: "No, you are not charged with anything yet". Then I said: "Why am I in this cell and why am I in prison? This was an awful cell and why should I be here if I had not been charged?" He said: "Well, we will see; it will take some time, but would you like to be in a room with other women?" I said: "What other women?" He said: "Why do you ask what other women?" I said: "Well, I would not like to be with somebody who is killer or a criminal." He said: "No, no, no, no. They are all women from Vukovar". I said: "Oh, in that case, yes, I would like to be with them". So they took me, first of all, for an examination to a Colonel who said his name was Branko, but he never gave his second name, an elderly man, and he had not a camouflage uniform but an ordinary uniform, because all that time they were changing uniforms from regular uniforms to camouflage uniforms and back. Anyway, that Branko started to examine me; who am I; where I came from; what am I; whether I was married; where I had lived -- the usual questions. Then he explained to me that I would have to write a statement about the situation in Vukovar. So they brought me back to the room in which there were some -- there were 52 other women from Vukovar in that room at that time. As soon as I entered, they recognised me because I knew some of them too. Most of these women were from the Mitnica district of Vukovar. So when Mitnica was evacuated, their men were taken to prison; the women actually came with their sons and husbands and remained in the prison. There were also women with children. There was an old woman who was alone, who had nobody. So when they took, when they captured the part of a city, they usually took men, God knows where, but they took the women to Mitrovica. So when I came among these women, I felt better. I could at least change my clothes and then sleep, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, I would like to show you, if I may, a short excerpt on the video. This is exhibit 23, a part of exhibit 23, if your Honours please. This is just a part of that exhibit. When you see it, doctor, if you could see parts of it that you recognise and that you would wish to speak about, if you would just give me a signal and then we will stop at it and we will talk at that point. So could you just watch the video that is being shown now? As it is being shown, tell us about what you recollect from seeing this video that is being played to you. It will be necessary for you to put on your video monitor, I believe. So might that part of exhibit 23 please now be shown to the witness? (Extract of video is played)

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Let me just explain. What you see now, before that -- can we see the beginning because that was .....

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could just stop there for a moment?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: If you could return just a little bit more. Can we go back a little bit more? You see this, this is the hole through which that heavy bomb, the aircraft bomb, fell which did not explode that I was telling you about earlier. That was the hole in the roof, then through the attic and through all the floors, all the way to the cellar to the nuclear shelter, and fell on to that bed where the patient was lying, and the technician actually was taking -- took this picture and wanted to get the sky. What you see, the yellow is the sky.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if it could be played on?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: These are patients that were lying there on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Stop just there, please.

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: The doctor behind me is a man from Zagreb, anaesthesiologist. So this was a very small room next to the plaster room where we used to come, take a break when we had a moment of respite and then we could talk there. We also had our lunches or dinners there and so on. Sometimes we even sang.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is very obvious, but the lady in the front is yourself, I take it?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: That is me, yes. Perhaps they could play on. This was Dr. Stanko, a physiologist, from Zagreb. What we saw were our medical rooms hit by grenades. These are nurses with patients on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: And this is the bomb, this is the bomb, maybe just a little bit back or maybe you cannot change this. The bomb is actually lying on the bed and the patient was there, and when the Police Inspector came to check, this was on 5th October 1991 -- you see the date -- the Inspector looked at this and found that the bomb was not dangerous, it would not explode. Then they took the piece of wire and pulled it because it was very, very heavy and they transferred it on to stretchers and took it out of the room on the stretchers. What you see there, the fragments, are the parts of the bed, the hospital bed. The patient was lucky to have survived. Now you can see what the bed looks like. The patient was a Serb, Peravu Kacni, an elderly man, who had been wounded, who was lying in hospital, and later I heard that he stayed in Vukovar and is, in fact, even now living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So it can be played on.

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Now, again this was what you see from the hole, looking down. This is the corridor and through this corridor you could walk to the air raid shelter. There were patients in that corridor. These are our ambulance vehicles you can see, and this is now the preparation for evacuation. That was taken after I had left. While I was there, the nurses and the children with the nurses were still in hospital. This is a nurse, Jurja, from the paediatric department of our hospital, but I was not there at that time when this was taken. They are leaving here now, but there are no technicians, laboratory technicians, no drivers. They are all women now and children, as you can see. Now they are all leaving through the main gate, and this is the gate through which I left when I left. Now they are moving towards -- they are moving towards the main entrance. There you can see the vehicles, the cars, that had been damaged. This is no longer the hospital. That is something else. That is some other evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, doctor, I think that after 18 days you were exchanged; is that right? You were released?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: After 18 days in Mitrovica, I first spent three days in the military investigation prison in Belgrade, and then I was exchanged, because in Belgrade I was questioned again, but that was real prison. Everything was according to the rules. That is where I spent three days. There I was with the whole group because they at that point, after 18 days, they prepared the group for exchange which consisted of doctors, medical staff, priests and some more civilians and my husband was in that same group, and that is when I saw him for the first time after so much time. I saw him on the bus when we were being taken from Mitrovica to Belgrade. I saw that he was still alive and that he was there. I had been informed earlier by some people that he was alive, and that he was also in Mitrovica at the same time, because he was taken from Borovo Naselje -- that is another story, of course, because there, Borovo Naselje, they totally destroyed our reserve hospital, our back-up hospital. There was a white flag with a red cross painted on it, but they brought the guns and trained their guns on to that building. They also dropped gas grenade, and so everybody started coming out, patients, wounded people and so on. My husband was there and then he left, then he was taken via Dalj to Kamanica and then to Stajicevo camp, and then I heard from a woman that he was there. I asked for the International Red Cross to come to Mitrovica and they came about eight days after our arrival. In Mitrovica we actually heard that some wounded people had been brought there, and that only 174 wounded people had arrived in Croatia. So we hoped that the rest of the wounded people were in Mitrovica. Later, when we came to Croatia, we found out that they were not the same wounded people; they were only a few people from our hospital, while the majority of them were from Borovo Naselje, and that our wounded people, our laboratory technicians, our civilians, including my father-in-law, that these people were not there. I was questioned in Belgrade for three days in that prison, as I told you, military prison. There was a prosecutor there, there was an investigating judge, and they asked me whether I would like to have a court appointed lawyer or whether I have a lawyer that I will appoint myself. I said: "I cannot decide anything. I have to ask the Minister of Health in Zagreb because I am a doctor and I have no idea about these procedures. I do not understand the law. I do not know what I am charged with". They said that it would take some time, that I might be exchanged sooner if they decide not to press any changes against me. So I said: "OK, I do not need any lawyer, any defence counsel", but they insisted and they called a lawyer, a military lawyer, a young man who came from a military legal institute in Belgrade and they said: "Now you will be a court appointed lawyer for this woman, for this doctor who is here." He had no idea who I am, and why he was brought there. I do not really know why they staged it like that, but they examined me, questioned me, all afternoon, although I had written in Mitrovica in my own hand, 118 pages, describing the situation in Vukovar, what was happening, from the beginning of the war until I left. But they questioned me again about the same things and they said that they had some serious indications, that they might press charges against me, that they would consider this, because I was publicly speaking on the telephone on fax accusing the Yugoslav army as an aggressor. I said: "I can admit that freely and I have the letters, I have copies, because that was the truth because they did actually for three months performed an act of aggression against us". The prosecutor, the one who acted as a prosecutor, he said: "Well, we have some more evidence against you and in connection with some doctors", and then they showed me a piece of paper from a doctor, because I sent two doctors Dr. Kosmanovic and Dr. Emedi, I sent them from our hospital to Borovo Komerz to organise a hospital there, and I issued them an order to do this so -----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you subsequently charged when you were there?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No, no. Eventually, they said I should go back to my room and that they will tell me in the evening whether I would be charged or not. In the evening they came to us again. They asked me to give an interview for television, B independent television, they said, and they decided that I was not going to be charged. So, the following morning they put us all -- exchanged us all, prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. I would turn to my two colleagues to ask whether they have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Doctor, could you tell us, did someone organise during the war any military action from the hospital against the JNA or in any way took part in the war from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No, never, never. There was no one like that because at that time the Croatian army had no real organisation at that time. There was a headquarters from which I sent my fax messages, because that was the only place where the fax machine was operating at all times, but nobody from the hospital was involved. Across the street from the hospital was the Police Station with the policemen, but in the hospital itself, there was nobody and we were quite apart from where the armies were. We often would go to the top floor and we watched, and we could see quite a long distance. We saw where the battle lines were; we could actually see the lines of supply that could -- but nobody came and the army did not want to compromise the hospital and that is why they never came to the hospital. There were only wounded people in the hospital, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, according to that, you did not have any kind of weapon inside your hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No. Police Inspector, Branko Lukinda, he was in charge of recording the wounded people when they arrived, to take the uniform from the wounded soldier and he took the uniform and the weapons to the Police every day. There may have been a gun or two which I did not know because the hospital was a large complex. There may be a man who had personal weapons which I did not know. We sometimes checked on the patients and on the wounded people. When, for instance, the commanders would come to visit their wounded soldiers, they were asked to leave all their weapons at the entry gate, and we told them never to give any weapons to the wounded people, to the patients, because it is dangerous in the hospital and weapons were not to be held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you were released, did anyone tell you what happened with the people who were at the hospital in November, 19, 18, what happened with those people?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: When I left the prison I worked for the Ministry of Health and the medical school in Zagreb. There we had a department, an office, that was gathering evidence or statements from the medical staff, from doctors, from nurses and so on. So they asked me and I went there to reconstruct the whole situation, to see who is there, who is missing and so on, because people who came to Zagreb immediately, nurses and doctors, they noticed that some people were missing. There were some wounded people who were missing, some patients. My mother-in-law and my sons noticed that I was missing, that my husband was missing. So when I arrived we checked on people who I knew and who were not around. We, for instance, looked at the medical staff, the drivers, their families and we investigated all the time to try to see who was missing and where they could be. We could not decide where they could be at all until in May 1992, I was travelling a lot at that time, I went to Brussels. I spoke to Monsieur Kouchner from France, who was the French Minister of Humanitarian Affairs, who was trying to organise a convoy for Vukovar. I met also representatives of the Medicines Sans Frontier. I visited Lord Carrington in London. I checked with all these people, so to speak, asking them for help, to identify where these people could be. I told Lord Carrington: "Look, some people are missing. There is the camp called Stajicevo, not far from Zrenjanin". That is where my husband had been kept. Lord Carrington was very excited. He said: "I do not know what I can do. I will go and talk to Slobodan Milosevic in Serbia or to Switzerland", I do not know, but he said he was afraid he could not do anything because Milosevic would say everything is not true. Then I said: "Ask Mr. Milosevic to take you to Zrenjanin to the Stajicevo camp", this is in Vojvodina in Serbia, "and there you could see that there are people there”. My husband was brought to Mitrovica from that camp and was then later exchanged later". Three days later we heard that the Stajicevo camp had been closed and people who were still alive were taken to Mitrovica and Nis, but that was a real concentration camp. It was a farm turned into a concentration camp, like later in Bosnia. Lord Carrington knew this. Then I spoke to Mr. Vance on 15th January 1992. I showed my complete list of all wounded people that we were looking for and I gave him the list, but we never had any response to our appeals or our requests. In May 1992, it was the first time that people were began to be exchanged from the Yugoslav prison. The Vukovar people began to be exchanged from the Yugoslav prisons and then we had the first witnesses, witnesses from Ovcara. There was Mr. Guncevic who used to work in the hospital. He was an economist and, anyway, he came to hospital to be evacuated. Then Mr. Zakovic who was a Red Cross worker. They were released and they told us about the Ovcara camp. That was the first we knew that. They told us they had been taken by bus to the barracks. They had spent some time in the army barracks and then were transferred to the Ovcara camp. They told us what kind of life they had there; how they were beaten. They recognised some people who had earlier been on the hospital staff, and Mr. Zakovic told me that that was the last time that he saw my father-in-law sitting on straw, on a heap of straw. Now, these two people, witnesses, and some others who you will probably hear, they were actually saved by some Serbs who took them to another camp, who took them to -- they were in Mitrovica, in Nis and, finally, they came here. But most of these people who had been taken away who were there with us on the morning of the 20th of November never actually appeared again, and we do not know where they are. They are missing. We are looking for them in all kinds of ways. There are many wives in Croatia whose husbands or sons were lost. There is a non-governmental organisation called "The Vukovar Mothers" who is searching for them, not only for them, also for other missing people. From Vukovar, Borovo Naselje and Eastern Slavonia, 1,280 people are missing, and the largest group from one single place is the hospital group. In this group there were four young men who were 16 years old at that time; a son of one of our cleaning women, and a husband who was suffering from cancer, an elderly man, and he had a tracheostomy. So that many members, many families, lost their members. 18 staff, technical staff, of the medical centre are missing, drivers, laboratory technicians. This is a very difficult tragedy, and both the parents and the medical staff actually hold me sort of responsible because I was responsible for the hospital and they think I can do for them something to find these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, may I ask you what happened with your mother?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: My mother was with the father-in-law. The father-in-law is still missing while -- my mother and my father-in-law remained in the hospital when the children and women left. The two of them remained, and my mother was waiting for me to come back and when the last wounded people were being transferred, then a doctor, Dr. Ivankovic, a Serb, told her (because he knew her as my mother), he said: "Look, if you intend to leave, leave now because God knows whether Vesna would ever come back or not, if you would like to go to Zagreb, do go to Zagreb now". So he put them into a transport of wounded people so that they left the hospital with the last transport on the evening of Wednesday, and they left for Mitrovica. That part of the convey was taken to Mitrovica. They spent the time in Mitrovica in the sports hall, in the gymnasium, and on the following day they were brought via Bosnia to Croatia for this free part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, allow me just to tire you for another five minutes because I know you are already very tired, and we thank you very much for this long testimony. The first thing I want to just make sure of is how far was Vukovar itself bombarded by the air raids? The hospital was part of Vukovar and the bombardment, as you mentioned, was the shelling was all over Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The hospital, I just add, you said they used parachute objects with powder, poisonous powder, and gas and the hospital itself received something like bombs of 250 kilogrammes which means that the hospital had a bigger share of the bombarding; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Although the hospital had an indication that it was a hospital and anybody shelling the city could know that it is a hospital ---

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: -- is that right? Do you think they had any reasons to do that?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned to Judge Odio-Benito that all those who were in the hospital were not armed, but did you have any previous formal resistance in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Only wounded, wounded people. We only had wounded people, those who had been wounded. The hospital only had wounded people, patients, and the two Inspectors of the Police who came to take records. We had no armed people in the hospital as a hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have any military objectives just beside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Nothing like canons against aircraft or anything?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Nothing like that?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No. I walked through the city quite a lot because I was sending the fax from the Headquarters which was not quite -- I walked to my home across the cemetery and so on. I moved around the city, but I never saw any guns or anything by the way of artillery. Let me also add that at that time the defenders of Vukovar had very few weapons. They may have had one or two guns, canons, artillery, but that was on the battle front in Dubrava in the Borovo Naselje district because this is far away from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned that you had the opportunity, when you went to Negoslavci, you went to the headquarters and met Colonel Mrksic, is that right, to arrange the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I went there to establish contact with the International Red Cross and the EC monitors, European Community monitors, because on the day before the EC monitors called me by phone and said: "We are calling from Negoslavci".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You noticed when you met Mrksic that he is the responsible person and he is the one who could do things, who could run the whole situation -- was that your impression?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes. You see, I had that information from General Raseta. General Raseta, Andrija Raseta, was the Commander of the 5th army district of the Yugoslav People's army in Zagreb at that time, and he was speaking on behalf of the Yugoslav People's army and he signed an agreement to neutralise the hospital, to make it neutral, to declare it neutral, and to evacuate the hospital under the supervision of the EC monitors and the International Red Cross. The agreement exists, his signature exists, and I think you have it in your documentation. You have a copy of that. He told me on the phone that Colonel Milan Mrksic was responsible for the implementation of this in the district of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in the hospital you met Sljivancanin, as you mentioned, and he asked you for the lists of the patients; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes. He was there together with the representative of the International Red Cross, Mr. Nicolas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he give you the strong impression that he was the one who is directing the whole thing, or was there someone else?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: My impression was that he was in charge in the field, because he in he was in the hospital. Colonel Mrksic was in the Headquarters. Negoslavci is about seven to eight kilometres away from the hospital. While Major Sljivancanin came that afternoon and stayed in the hospital, and he would come in and out and so on, so he was actually conducting and was in charge of the evacuation of the civilians. I had the impression that he brought the International Red Cross representatives and that he was responsible in the field. That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you come across Radic?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No -- or I may have, but I did not know the name. I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When Sljivancanin made his lists, was there any criterion to distinguish the several lists from one another, except the one you mentioned, that the doctors, the medical staff, were separate? Did they choose young people, old people? Was there any criterion?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No, no, I do not think they made any lists that evening at all because they took our lists, and our lists had just the name, surname, diagnosis, and where the patient would like to be evacuated to. That was all the information the list contained. But our Administrative Officer and a nurse made a list of the medical staff because we did not have that list. I never heard that the Yugoslav army or the International Red Cross made their own lists. They only took my list of patients, of wounded people, and I am not aware of them making their own lists. I heard later, and you might hear it from other witnesses, that when they brought these people to the Ovcara camp they took their documents and then started to make lists. I heard later from one of our clerical staff who remained in Vukovar, who remained for several months later in Vukovar, and came to Croatia later -- her name is Slavica Baraz and she is now in the free part of Croatia -- she came to me and said: "When you had all left, then the doctors, Serbs" asked her to continue working in the hospital because she was a specialist in something she knew. She saw a box full of documents and identification papers, and she said she saw the identity cards of my father-in-law on top of that pile. She asked what kind of documents were they, and she was told that these documents go to Belgrade and she should not go through them. So, I believe that when they got these people, they took their documents and they realised who was present there. They did not make any list beforehand. I heard from my head nurse that they brought only a list of 18 patients, wounded patients, whose names were called first, and some of these people are now still listed as missing. These were more serious patients with grave wounds, but we never heard that these more seriously wounded people were in Ovcara. They probably were not in Ovcara and we do not know where they were taken and how they are missing, in what sense they are missing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned there are 2,800 people missing. Did I get this number right?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: 2,800 from the whole of Croatia, but from Vukovar, 1,280, 1,280 from Vukovar, Borovo, Ilok. That is the eastern part of Croatia which is still under occupation. 1,280 people missing. From Vukovar itself, some 300 people are missing from the hospital; about 100 people are missing from Borovo Naselje; some 50 from the Velepromet group. So, at every point where evacuation was made, there were some missing people, civilians and wounded people, and we still do not know where these people are now. We have some evidence, some eyewitness reports, of mass graves but for none of these, apart from Ovcara, do we have any confirmation because we can only rely on what we hear from people who were eyewitnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So if you consider that 1,280 people are just missing from Vukovar, and the total amount is 2,800, it means that Vukovar was very heavily damaged and distressed and lost, perhaps, more than one-third of -- composes almost more than one-third of the people missing?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: This is true. Vukovar, which you can see, there is a book called "Mass Killing" (and I have few copies here), you can see what the share of Vukovar was in the total war against Croatia in 1991/92. It is difficult to give you statistics because I do not remember them all and I am rather tired, but out of a total number of wounded in the whole of Croatia, one-third are wounded people in Vukovar. Out of the total number of killed people, Vukovar accounts, there are some 7,000 people who were killed in the whole of Croatia. In the whole of Croatia there is some 7,000; out of this, according to our knowledge of what we know when we were there, there were about 1,100 people killed and some close to 1,300 are missing. If these are also killed, then we have 2,400 people killed, which is one-third of the whole of Croatia, and Vukovar is very small area. It is a small area which had 164 square kilometres, 84,000 population. This is the part which has been disproportionately damaged and suffering in the whole of Yugoslavia. Sarajevo was damaged, Bosnia was badly damaged, but nowhere do you find such a heavy concentration of suffering. This is 10 by three kilometres. Over three months you had more than 9,000 missiles falling on to the city. During that time we had underground 15,000 people living in underground shelters, women, children; 30,000 -- 30 per cent of them Serbs because Vukovar was a multi-ethnic town. So, the Serbs themselves, when they entered Vukovar, when we started coming out in the barracks, Marin Vivic and I, and an officer came and said: "Is it possible that so many people survived?" They could not even believe that so many people could survive such heavy shelling. Vukovar is an awful tragedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it by any chance a military centre or was it one of the -----

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Not at all. No, no, it was not a military centre at all. At that time in the former Yugoslavia, Vukovar was a small town on the banks of the Danube that was always the most eastern most part of Croatia. Ilok is, perhaps, more to the east. Ilok had some 90 per cent of Croats, some Slovaks, Ruthenians and a few Serbs. Vukovar was 35 kilometres to the west of Ilok, but it always through the centuries probably from, I do not know, 200 years ago, it had always been the meeting point, a cross-roads, of various cultures. The Vucedol culture dates back to many centuries before Christ, and later during the feudal times and during Turkish invasions in the First and Second World War, this area was always a place where the -- at the cross-roads between east and west, north and sort, and in the former Yugoslavia this was an area where people lived in very mixed communities. 30 per cent of marriages were mixed marriages. 43.8 per cent were Croats; 37 per cent were Serbs; 1.5 per cent Hungarians, and there were also some who declared themselves Yugoslavs, they were seven per cent. The town of Vukovar was the centre and mostly Croatian. Before the war, Vukovar had 45,000 population. This was a whole. Borovo Naselje was its industrial district. The villages in the direction of Osijek were mainly Serbian villages, Borovo Selo, Bobota, Trpinja, Brsadin; towards the east were Croatian villages. When the whole fighting started in October, there was shooting, they started hitting Tovanic and Ilok. People were afraid and they saw that they had no chance of survival there. So, they started negotiating with the European, with the European monitors, and under their protection they left Ilok. For instance, the whole of Ilok, all Croats, had to leave Ilok. This was the first example of ethnic cleansing in October 1991. We heard this on television, and we were very unhappy about this, about Ilok, but we did not want to leave Vukovar. Vukovar, we thought, we cannot leave; this is our town. Nobody has any right or any reason to drive us out. So, the Serbs remained there as well, not all of them, some left perhaps. But later, some other Serbs came with the Yugoslav army, but most local Serbs were still there. When you look at the lists of people who were killed by the grenades, there were many Serbs who were killed. They started shooting in August with several grenades every week, and they wanted us to empty the city, to behave like Ilok. We refused. Then they took us and occupied us at all cost, and we survived it all. We knew that this was a war and that we had to hold out. What happened later, what people suffered later, the civilians, women who left -- who lost members of their families and what they went through later after occupation of Vukovar, that was horrible because in the cellars you would find some 70 people living. In the one shelter there were 700 people, all of them mixed Croats and Serbs together, and they all waited for the day to come when they could live in peace again. But when the Yugoslav army came and the Chetniks came, then they said: "No, Croats on one side; Serbs on the other side", and they took this group in one direction, the other group in another direction, and that was when the true consequences of the war began to be felt and these people are still missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sure that you are very tired, Mrs. Bosanac. We will not prolong this hearing, but I would like to ask you a simple impression that you have. When you go back to this story of the hospital, do you feel this was a concerted plan, an organised, a premeditated plan? I am talking about the disappearance of the people who were under your responsibility and authority?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I do not know. It is very difficult for me to say. I see no reason, I see no logic, in separating these people, you see, because there were children there, there were wounded soldiers, the Croatian soldiers, there were some elderly people, people who were weak, civilians. I see no criterion. The only thing was that they said all men should go out. So, all men left, as my mother-in-law told me, and they put them on to buses and took them away. Some of them were brought back, in fact. Some nurses realised that their husbands were missing, so they came with the list to Sljivancanin and asked for these people to be returned, and some people who had identification papers on them as drivers of the medical centre and so on. So 15 were brought back from the barracks. They were brought back on a bus, but the others were taken somewhere else, and I think that people who were in Ovcara, your witnesses, will be able to tell you more. But I personally see no criterion as to how these people were separated and how they were classified. Also, people who are missing from Vukovar, from Borovo, quite a number are civilians and young girls, women, children, elderly people. There is no visible criterion that you will say: "Well, somebody was a fighter and was treated differently". I think that some criterion must have been there, but what they were is beyond me, but they were always Croats, non-Serbs. It has for generations been like that, that the same families are attacked and they suffer. In 1945, for instance, my father-in-law's two brothers were taken away and they were lost. Now from the hospital my father-in-law was taken away, and his nephew, the husband of the man who was taken away in 1945 -- the son of the man who was taken away in 1945. There are other family histories that connected what happened now with what had happened in 1945 and what would probably happen again in the next war in 50 years time, unless a solution is found. I was born in 1949. We lived in the former Yugoslav. I grew up in the former Yugoslavia, but I knew what the war is -- I did not know what war was, and I never experienced a Second World War and I had to experience it now, although I never expected it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac, the Tribunal would like to thank you. Do you have the impression that you were able to say everything that you wanted to the Tribunal, to answer all of the questions asked by the Prosecutor, and the several additional questions that the judges asked? Do you have the feeling that you were able to express yourself fully as to what you intended to do? Do you have the feeling that you would like to conclude by saying something else; if you do, would you tell us, otherwise say what would you like before going back to your country.

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: It is difficult to say much. Whenever I speak about Vukovar, I speak a lot and I never feel I have said enough. You see, this part of the country was very badly destroyed during these few months, and now after five years, five years later, I can only say that it is a great pity that the international community had not reacted sooner, because, possibly, had the IFOR or UNTAES, or some other forces, European monitors, that would have been effective, had they arrived in August 1991 in Vukovar with enough political pressure against Milosevic and the Yugoslav army, they would have, perhaps, had an effect. They would have not -- they would have prevented destruction and killing, and I think probably in that case the war in Bosnia would have been prevented as well. So this is my general message, if I may say so, that one should be better informed and that one should react as soon as possible to protect people. We expected a great deal from the international community. We thought that they had the convoy of the Medicines Sans Frontier would bring us infusions and medical supplies, and they would take our wounded people as long as we have wounded people. That was the agreement and they promised this, but the Yugoslav army did not allow them. They did not allow a single aspirin to be brought to our hospital, not a single infusion. They took a group of patients and that was all. The aggressor is always obeyed -- he has to be obeyed probably -- and people who need to be helped do not get helped. I apologise for such emotional words and it would take a long time to tell you everything about Vukovar. There are some books even in English and perhaps you might find it interesting if you have the time to go through them and read them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac, the Tribunals thank you. It is very sensitive for you having come and wishes you a good and calm journey home, and hopes that you will find the serenity that you need, if it is possible. The Usher can accompany the witness out. Once the witness has left the courtroom we will suspend the session for 10 minutes before we resuming. Thank you. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will resume at 5.30. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (Adjourned for a short time).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecuting Counsel, we are going to introduce the next witness. Are you making a request for any particular protection? I notice that the Registrar is ready. Prosecutor, would you please introduce the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. At this time we will call Dr. Neda Striber as the next witness. We are requesting protective measures for this witness. The sole measure we are asking for is that her image be altered and that the gallery not be able to observe her as she enters the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Registrar, firstly, would you please note in the minutes of this hearing, according to a well-known procedure, that we have undertaken an amendment to the proceedings for the hearing for the next witness who wishes that her identity not be concealed, but that the Prosecutor has requested that the image of the witness which can be broadcast through the media be completely concealed. Before showing in the witness it is, therefore, necessary to lower the screens in order that the public not be able to identify the face of Dr. Striber, following which then we can bring up the screens again. Are you quite sure that there is no possibility of seeing through? There are no problems? Mr. Registrar, could you please ask the Usher to show in the witness who will then introduce herself. Dr. Neda Striber, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Madam, firstly can you hear in your mother tongue what I am saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you tuned in to the right channel? If so, please introduce yourself and then the solemn oath, the solemn statement which the Usher has given to you, your family name, your first name, your age and your profession.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Neda Striber. I was born in 1960. I am a doctor specialised in opthamology. I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, madam. Kindly be seated. Do you feel comfortable to make your statement, give your testimony? Do you feel quite comfortable? You are appearing before an International Tribunal which at the request of the Prosecutor is ready to listen to you. Do you feel calm and tranquil? Prosecutor, the floor is yours, your questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Dr. Striber, you indicated that you are doctor specialising in the field of opthamology, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long have been working as an opthamologist?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: For the past four years. I would like to apologise. I passed my specialisation exam in 1994. I would like to apologise because I did not give you a correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is all right. How long have you been a physician?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I have worked since 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In 1991 where were you working?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Then I worked I started to work at the Opthamology Department at Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were your specific duties at the Vukovar Hospital at that time?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: At the beginning I worked with the whole department of the Opthamology Department. During 1990 when the situation changed completely, so at the end of the May 1991 I was the only physician of the Opthamology Department at Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You indicated that the situation changed at the end of May 1991. What had happened at the beginning of May which had led to an increase in tension in the area?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, at that time the first tensions started to emerge especially after the incident at Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did there come a time when this tension erupted into actual fighting between the Croats and the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: The first major incident with armed conflicts started to take place in July and in August of '91.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did this affect operations at Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Well, of course, the Vukovar Hospital had to adjust to these new circumstances, especially since the situation in the city of Vukovar changed completely. At the same time there were also changes within the hospital, because staff started to leave us, you know, people started to leave the city as the fighting started to intensify. Some people remained; other people decided to leave with their families. That was according to the individual assessment of each and everyone, whether one should stay or leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You indicated that some of the staff members began to leave, so there was a decrease in the total hospital staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, considerably. I could tell you approximately for our department, for instance, until the beginning of the war there were about 20 people working in our department, 18 or 19, I cannot give you the exact answer. At the beginning of the aggression we were just four including myself to work at this department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At the same time that there was a decrease in staff members, I take it that there was an increase in the number of patients who were coming into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, the number of patients was increasing every day. This was especially visible in August 1991. At that time we were receiving many more patients, i.e. wounded and, of course, working conditions were changed as well in the hospital. Due to the initial shelling of one part of the hospital we had to adjust to those new circumstances. Therefore, we tried to evacuate the upper parts of the hospital for security reasons, we tried to evacuate both staff and patients. As the fightings were intensifying, we were obliged to go to the lower part of the hospital. So at the beginning of September '91 we moved definitely to the cellar of the new and old part of the hospital and we also opened the atomic shelter where we would put patients and wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You indicated that the hospital had been hit from the shelling. Was it hit on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: At the beginning the shelling was less intensive and we did not think that it would really continue, but during the fightings the hospital was constantly exposed to the shelling. Every day we would receive more and more shellings, so there were some days where you could not even go out to the hospital compound, let alone to count all the mortars that would hit the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Over the course of the three months in which the battle of Vukovar went on, what was the result in terms of damage to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: We were directly hit, the building was directly shelled, so the building of the new hospital was completely destroyed. You could see that on a lot of photos that were taken after the fall. The old hospital was also hit, so it means that the whole construction of the old hospital was in fact destroyed. They were no windows on those facilities and there were certain parts of the hospital that could not be used at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the time when the battle was going on were you able to move around freely within the city?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Well, that was always risky. Every time when you would step out there was always 50 per cent of a chance that you would come back and 50 per cent of a chance that you would get killed. I mean it was at your own risk that you would go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to go to your home at all during the battle?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: At the beginning I would go back home. I would always wait until a decrease in the fighting, until there were less shells, but at the end of August and at the beginning of September '91 all the staff, all the medical staff in fact moved to the hospital. So we literally lived and worked all the time in the hospital. A lot of staff also brought their family members, their children with them, because they just could not go back home. Their houses, they could not use any more their homes either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: OK. What happened to your family?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I took my children out of the town somewhere around mid-September, so my children were not with me, my husband neither.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you continued to stay in Vukovar to continue working in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As the battle continued, did conditions at the hospital deteriorate?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, the situation deteriorated. We had more and more wounded people coming and at the same time we ran out of water and electricity. These were really very specific conditions of work; these were not normal working conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By the middle of November what was the situation like in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: At the middle of November 1991 the hospital was literally fully booked, every single centimetre of space was occupied. There were a lot of patients, wounded people, civilians. There were a lot of staff with their family members, with their children. This situation at certain moments was really critical because there were just too many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As the fall of the city to the JNA became imminent, did you see other people from Vukovar coming to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: In the last days of the battle more and more people, more and more civilians began to come to the hospital. I cannot remember exactly the date, I think it was in the afternoon when the civilians, at least I had a feeling that those civilians were coming from all parts of the city, for the first time in fact we realised how many civilians there were left in the city. There was a whole river, a flood of civilians, of people that were coming into the hospitals and they were looking for the refuge in the hospital. These were elderly people, mothers with small children. They wanted to be safe in the hospital. It is very difficult to say how many people there were in the hospital at that time. Those people would not say anything. They would not ask for anything. They were just begging for a little bit of space where they could take refuge. You know, it is very difficult to say, to describe how it looked like. Every single inch was filled. It was dark and there was only this flood of people that was entering the hospital. We did not have any food. We did not have water. We did not have anything to give these people. I remember one grandmother said to me: "But look, my child, we are not looking for anything; we are just looking for a safe place."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In your estimate, approximately how many people had gathered at the hospital by the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: By the 19th of November there were definitely more than 1,000 people. I cannot say exactly the number, but definitely more than 1,000.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were they located? Were they inside the building, outside?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Most of them were within the hospital itself, but since the hospital was so occupied and people could not enter the hospital, I really have the impression that a lot of people stayed within the hospital compound, which means outside of the hospital itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During this time period, especially near the end of the battle, did you see any Croatian soldiers in uniform at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Towards the end of the battle, well, you know, Croatian soldiers would come to pay a visit to their friends in the hospital, they would always come to see them, so there was always someone coming in the hospital. I cannot say whether at that particular moment there were people who were visiting patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see anyone carrying weapons at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you please clarify your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers carrying weapons or anyone at all bringing weapons into the hospital, guns?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Do you mean during the last days or do you mean in general, during the whole period of the battle?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: First of all, during the whole period of the battle and then specifically near the end, at the end of the battle as the city was about to fall.

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: All of the patients and all of the fighters that were wounded and they were coming in the hospital, they always had to leave their weapons, their guns, at the entry of the hospital. There was a person in charge of recording the weapons. I do not know where those weapons were kept later on, but as patients, in their capacity as patients, they were not in possession of weapons. I cannot say of course that maybe someone did not have a weapon or a gun, but there was an instruction that new weapons should be kept in the hospital. The soldiers that would come to pay a visit to someone, they had weapons because they would enter with their weapons and also go out with their weapons. During the last days it is sure that none of those who were there had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did there come a point in time when JNA soldiers arrived at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: As far as I know, the first time I saw the JNA soldiers was on the 19th of November in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any resistance given to these JNA soldiers by anyone in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: OK. These first JNA soldiers that arrived there, how did they behave?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I would not say that they approached any of the staff or patients at that time. They would simply establish contact with our Hospital Crisis Committee, that is to say with our Director. On the 19th of November in the evening, late afternoon or evening I believe, I do not remember exactly the hour, you will understand it because the time just stopped for us, but on the 19th of November several JNA soldiers walked through the hospital and they were looking at the patients and at the hospital and I remember their comment, they said: "It is really impossible. We cannot believe that they are working under such conditions."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you spend the night of the 19th of November to the morning of the 20th ?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: We did not know what would happen during that night. Nobody was able to tell us what was going to happen the following day. We were expecting an evacuation of the patients and the wounded, because we were constantly told that such a thing would happen. We were expecting, you know, to receive instructions how to prepare our wounded, because we heard that there have been some negotiations about the evacuation of the hospital. People were afraid, they did not know what would happen. There was a certain chaos because we were all trying to do something. We were all taking care of the wounded, but we were also all very afraid how the evacuation due to happen the following day would really happen. The nurses continued with their regular work. They were preparing the wounded for the evacuation that was agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you stay that night?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I spent that night in my room, in my medical room, which is a space where we all lived together. It is a room that has 12 or maybe up to 15 square metres and it is situated in the cellar of the old part of the hospital. There were four, sorry, there were nine of us living there. This was our medical room, but this was also a room where we would reside throughout the war. It is a very limited space with a concrete floor. We had some mattresses on the floor. We tried to sleep on those mattresses. There was a very, very small hole, sort of windows, but there were no glasses or net; there were just planks, wooden planks put on that hole. We tried to protect ourselves from the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Early on the morning of the 20th of November did you see the head nurse for any reason?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Excuse me, you ask me about the 20th?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, it is on the morning of the 20th.

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: A little bit before 7 a.m. on the 20th of November the head nurse came to our medical room (or as I would call it our living room). She came with the list accompanied by a military person. She called out one of my patients who during that time was in this limited space. They asked him to step out in the corridor. This person in military uniform, I assume he was a physician because he said to me: "Dear colleague, would you please tell me what were the injuries?" He wanted to know whether these were heavily or light bodily injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the name of this man that they called out?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: It was Josip Bradaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No, I did not. I know just that he was taken out of this space somewhere outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After this contact with the head nurse, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: The head nurse said to us that there is an order that all medical staff should gather in one part of the hospital for a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did there meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: It took place in the surgery ward which was, in fact, the former plaster room of the emergency department. There were doctors, nurses and all other staff of the hospital were present at this meeting. Major Sljivancanin invited us to this meeting and that was when he introduced himself to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was he the person who was in charge of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, he was in charge of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he say to all of you?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Well, I am afraid I am not able to repeat every single word that was said by Major Sljivancanin, but it was more or less like this: "Our doctors, Dr. Bosanac and Dr. Njavro -- your doctors, Dr. Bosanac and Dr. Njavro are not any more in charge of the hospital. We are taking over the hospital. The JNA army came here to liberate the city and the hospital." At the same time we were told that he understands that in our capacity of medical staff we were obliged to perform our duties, but each person who fought against JNA soldiers should be held accountable for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did this meeting last?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: It is very difficult to say this, but I would say it was during an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While the meeting was going on did you notice anything unusual occurring in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: At a certain point I left a group of the medical staff gathered in this meeting and I stepped out of the room, and at that moment I noticed some of our patients who could walk, they were going out accompanied by one of the soldiers towards one of the entries to the hospital, the entry to the emergency department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you finally did get out of the meeting, what did you observe in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: The patients left in the hospital. There was almost nobody left in the hospital. There were very, very few patients left in the first part of the hospital. There were just a couple of beds with some patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The patients that were remaining, were any of them men?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about with your patients, the patients that you were responsible for, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: On my return from the meeting I saw that none of my patients was there. I walked through all the rooms. I wanted to see how they were doing. I wanted to give them the last instructions for the evacuation, and I really believed that this was the beginning of the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many patients were under your care at that time?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Twenty-four patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At any point in time had you prepared a list of these patients?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: In the evening of the 19th of November, that was the last time when I went to take care of my patients to give them the medication that they would need during the evacuation the following day, and when I wanted to give them the instructions and tell them that we would be with them. I wanted to reassure them. During that visit I made the exact list of all the patients. I also made a list of their injuries with the exact description. I added also their address and I asked them where would they like to continue with their treatment, because, you know, in our areas we would sometimes send people for treatment to Zagreb or to Belgrade and it was always an individual decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At this time I would like to show what we have marked as Exhibit No. 27. Can you identify this document?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes. This is my handwriting and the information that it contains, this is my last list of patients that I made and submitted to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is this an original document?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I think it is a photocopy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does it appear to be an accurate photocopy of the original?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many names are contained in this list?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Twenty-four.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe what information you have listed next to each name?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Well, this is the first name and surname, then the kind of injury and the address of the patient and the place where that patient would like to continue his or her treatment, because these were mostly patients that needed further treatment in some kind of more specialised institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many of the patients that are on this list were men?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I think there were only two women on the list, if I am not mistaken, patient No. 8, madam Zahora, and then Mrs. Ostro Kata, Kata Ostro, and Mrs. Janka Potkorski, three women.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these patients still in their beds when you returned from the meeting?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Men not. They were absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But the three women were still there?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were all of the people there included on this list actually wounded?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I had two patients. One was a patient that was in our hospital in August and September 1991 and who had an impaired oratory canal, and at the moment of the evacuation he was already under control, so to speak. He was the husband of my head nurse and she asked me to keep him in hospital so that he could leave with us during the evacuation. Also there was another patient, a gentleman, who was the husband of one of my colleagues, Dr. Zego where again he was a member, so to speak, of the families of our staff and we had him also on the list. These were then husbands of two of our ladies who were working on our staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why had these men or their wives asked that they be included among the wounded?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: You see it is normal that one is concerned about their family members, and I in fact understand why these women decided that they should take their husbands with them as patients. This was fear, fear of the unknown. This was a desire to protect somebody who is a member of your family, but also it is a kind of thought which says, well, if you have a patient, the patient will be protected, because there are all kinds of international conventions to protect patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They feared for their safety otherwise, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: We all were afraid for our safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to all of these men that were taken out of the hospital, that were removed from their beds that morning?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I know about the destinies of some of these people because they came to Zagreb and they were treated in Zagreb, but many of them are now listed as missing. We do not know what the criterion was that some patients were allowed to proceed to Zagreb and what was the criterion that some people were kept and are now listed as missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see any of these men again that day?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you see them being taken out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I did not leave the hospital compound. I only saw that they were being taken into the backyard of the hospital, but I was not allowed to go out of the hospital so I do not know where they were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Through which entrance to the building were they taken out of?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: We assumed, and I cannot claim that that is correct, they did not leave through the main gate, but rather through the side gate. This is the gate leading towards -- which is in the back part of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At any point during that morning did you see international monitors from the International Red Cross or the ECMM present at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: During that morning while we had the meeting and when the patients were being taken away, I am quite sure that there was no observer in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you later see monitors present at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Probably quite a lot of time elapsed and when we all decided where we would go and we were standing outside on the hospital ground, those of us who wanted to go to Zagreb, so it was several hours later then we saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By this time it was well after all of the men had been removed from the hospital, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, quite a long time after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the course of the morning of the 20th as people were being evacuated from the hospital, did you hear any shooting or explosions occurring anywhere in the area?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: On the 20th we heard no explosions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any shooting or any indication that fighting was still going on anywhere in the area of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At approximately what time did you leave the hospital that day?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Probably around noon. I cannot tell you the precise time, but it was around noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How were you taken out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: We spent -- once we decided rather to go to Zagreb which we were allowed to decide, we were standing in the hospital grounds for an hour or two hours. This was in front of our emergency admission room. This was, as I say, in the hospital grounds but outside in the open. After that we were told that buses were waiting. We left the hospital grounds and came to the part where the court building used to stand, and we saw buses parked there and we entered those buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As you were leaving the city of Vukovar, were you able to observe what had happened to the city over the past three months?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: You could not recognise the city any more. There was deadly silence and you could not even hear birds singing. It looked horrible. Trees were lying on the ground. The buildings, you could only surmise that they had been buildings. The centre of the city was totally destroyed. Also there were various parts of building materials lying on the street, parts of trees, big branches and tree trunks lying on the street in front of the department store. In the very centre of the city you could see through the -- you could see from the buses, you could see also people lying in front of that department store by the side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These people appeared to be dead?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, judging by the position of their bodies I would say they were dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to see them well enough to tell if they had been killed recently or had been there for a long period of time?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: You could see very well that they were corpses that had not been lying there for a long time. I would say that they looked, it is difficult to say, but they were people killed moments earlier or a couple of hours before. I cannot be precise but they were certainly not long-lying corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At this time, your Honours, I would like to tender Exhibit 27 to the court. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecution, I would like to give the floor to my colleagues. Judge Odio Benito.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, do you know why Sljivancanin talk about liberate the city and the hospital? Liberate from whom? What was the situation because it is a little strange to hear about liberation in this case. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: This was their vision of things. You see, all of the time in the Serbian media, as far as we could see, the JNA always said that they were liberating the city. We did not want to be liberated. We were there in our city. There was no need for any kind of liberation. We lived there normally. At least in our view it was a normal kind of life with our neighbours, with our friends. Nobody had to come and liberate us from anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
