utterances.text: Dr. Striber, you mentioned that crowds of people were asking for shelter in the hospital because they were afraid and they thought the hospital would give them some safety. Many of these people or some of them were resistant, do you think, or was it just the simple crowds of people, citizens of Vukovar? Were there some combatants, resistance among the people who took shelter in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I can tell you, when I saw people entering the hospital they were very, very ordinary people, common people, ordinary citizens of Vukovar, elderly people, women, children, who came for help or for safety or they thought was safety. So they were civilians quite definitely and they came to find -- but the second half of your question I lost, so could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I understood your answer. Some of your patients, were some of your patients among the resistants or the previous fighters? You said that you found when you came back to the rooms the men were not there any more. Were they, as you said simply patients or were they combatants and resistants who were being treated at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: You see for me at the moment of admission of a patient they were all simply patients and I would not then separate them into class, a class of patients, civilian patients and combatants, because all previous activities, if they had had any of which I was not even aware, that is the end of it. That is not something which I am concerned with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have anything to do with Sljivancanin? Did you have some contact with him and how do you assess his position in the hospital? Was he the man ruling the hospital or was there a director who managed the hospital and Sljivancanin was just staying aside?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Personally I did not have any direct contact with him apart from that meeting where everybody was present at the meeting, but my general impression, and the impression of all of us, was that he was the kind of person who was taking the hospital over, so to speak, that is how he appeared. He said: "Now I am in charge of hospital, all aspects of its operation, all aspects of its work." This was our impression and my impression personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So according to your assessment, you think that everything that happened in the hospital was under the authority of Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I would say that this is very probable. I would say that this is very probable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Dr. Striber, just a few points of clarification. The patients at the point of evacuation, were they brutally treated?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: In the course of evacuation I cannot tell you, but if this was evacuation, I do not know whether one could call this evacuation, but there was no maltreatment, at least I saw none.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you be able to say anything about how many people disappeared at Vukovar between the bombing, the shelling of the city, as well then later on as the disappearances from the hospital; the number of people who lost their lives, the number of disappeared persons, injured persons, have you heard about any figures?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: As far as I know, judging by the records that we have, there was something like 1,200 or 1,300, 1,200, 1,300, but during the fighting itself I would say that this figure includes, covers only people for which records are kept. The total number of those killed in the fighting again is known to the extent that we have records about them, people whose deaths were recorded in the hospital and so on. But I know for sure that after so much shelling and bombardment quite a number of people died, a very large number. Many civilians remained in their shelters, in their houses or in the remnants, the ruins of their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you are saying the number of disappeared persons from the hospital would be around 1,000 or 1,200. That is the only figure you are aware of. What exactly does this figure consist of? I am sorry this appears to be a question about accounting. It is very dramatic accounting of course, but this is an important point for the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Let me try to explain. From the hospital some 300 people are missing, but when I say 1,200, this is the total number of people missing from Vukovar, not from the hospital. I was not precise enough in my first statement.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Last question. What is the state of Vukovar at the present time? What is the dominant feeling in Vukovar? What is the situation in Vukovar, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I could not tell you that because for five years I have not been to the city. I left with a convoy and I can only see some pictures. I can see some documents or what you find on television, in the media and so on. This used to be a lovely city and today it is ruined.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Striber. The Tribunal is sensitive to the fact that you have come to give your testimony. It would like to thank you. I would like to issue a very calm and serene journey back following these events which you have experienced. Once again the Tribunal would like to thank you. Registrar, please take all necessary measures in order to ensure that the witness is protected, firstly, visually.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to thank you very much and thank you for your good wishes and kind words, but I would like to go back to my city. We all of us from Vukovar would like to go back in peace. There has been a lot of killing. There is a lot of people who have suffered and nobody would want to have the same experience repeated ever. It would be best if this could be done in peace.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, madam. If the Usher would show the witness out. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecution, we will recommence our hearing tomorrow morning at 9 a.m. to continue the hearing of the witnesses which you have requested should be heard at the Tribunal. So this hearing is adjourned and we will recommence tomorrow morning at 9 a.m.. The hearing is adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: (The hearing was adjourned for a short time)
